title: Amanta and purnimanta month conventions
description: Some Hindu lunisolar calendars delimit months from new moon to new moon (amanta) while others use full moon boundaries (purnimanta). These are documented calendrical conventions, not a single rule shared by every South Asian community.
source: Dershowitz, Nachum, and Edward M. Reingold. Calendrical Calculations, 4th ed., Cambridge University Press, 2018.
confidence: High for the named calendar conventions; regional practice varies.

title: Chinese lunisolar calendar
description: Traditional Chinese calendar months begin at astronomical new moon; intercalary months keep lunar months aligned with the solar year. Regional and historical calendar rules have changed, so this record is not a universal date-conversion service.
source: Dershowitz, Nachum, and Edward M. Reingold. Calendrical Calculations, 4th ed., Cambridge University Press, 2018.
confidence: High for the general calendrical rule; local conventions vary.

title: Islamic Hijri calendar
description: The Islamic calendar is lunar. Month-start practice can depend on crescent sighting or calculated criteria set by a community or authority; dates can differ, and this atlas does not issue religious calendar dates.
confidence: High for the calendar structure; month-start methods vary by authority.

title: Maya lunar tables in the Dresden Codex
description: Scholarly analysis of Maya codices documents lunar tables and eclipse-related reckoning. This record refers to a specific historical manuscript tradition, not to all Maya communities or a claim that the tables predicted terrestrial events.
source: Bricker, Victoria R., and Harvey M. Bricker. Astronomy in the Maya Codices. Memoirs of the American Philosophical Society, 2011.
confidence: Scholarly reference; interpretation of manuscript tables is specialized.

title: Maramataka
description: Te Ara describes maramataka as Māori lunar calendars connecting named nights and local seasonal knowledge. Practices and interpretations are iwi- and place-specific; this short entry does not reproduce restricted or sacred knowledge.
source: Te Ara — The Encyclopedia of New Zealand, “Māori lunar calendar — maramataka”; https://teara.govt.nz/en/maramataka-the-lunar-calendar
confidence: Published public reference; community variation is essential.

title: Metonic cycle
description: The 19-year cycle approximates 235 synodic months to 19 solar years and was used to reconcile lunar and solar calendars. It is a historical astronomical/calendar concept, not evidence that lunar events cause social events.
confidence: High for the cycle relationship; historic adoption varied.

title: Galileo publishes Sidereus Nuncius
description: Galileo's 1610 publication reported telescopic observations of lunar surface features, helping establish that the Moon has uneven terrain. The entry records a publication and observation history, not a lunar-caused terrestrial event.
source: Galileo Galilei, Sidereus Nuncius (Venice, 1610); digitized copies catalogued by major research libraries.
confidence: Primary historical publication; exact observing dates precede publication.

title: Apollo 11 lunar landing
description: Apollo 11's Lunar Module landed on the Moon on 1969-07-20 UTC. The date is a mission record; the lunar phase has no asserted causal link to the mission.

title: Tide-generating force and local tides
description: The Moon's differential gravitational attraction contributes to ocean tides; solar forcing also matters. Local water levels depend on basin geometry, bathymetry, coastline shape, weather, and resonance. This application does not compute tide heights or station predictions.
confidence: Established mechanism; local predictions require validated regional models and observations.

title: Spring and neap tide geometry
description: New/full moon alignments tend to produce larger tidal ranges (spring tides), while quarter phases tend to produce smaller ranges (neap tides). Local response differs substantially; phase geometry alone does not determine a site's water level.
confidence: Established broad pattern; not a local forecast.

title: Eclipses require orbital alignment
description: The Moon's orbit is tilted relative to Earth's orbital plane, so most new and full moons do not produce eclipses. Local visibility and circumstances require a specific eclipse ephemeris and geographic path data; those are not bundled here.
confidence: Established geometry; no local eclipse predictions in this release.

title: Claims about behavior, earthquakes, and disasters
description: This release does not provide predictive claims about human behavior, earthquakes, weather disasters, or other terrestrial events from lunar phase. A claim requires evidence for a specific mechanism, outcome, and context; no such prediction is implemented here.
source: USGS, “Can the position of the Moon or the planets affect seismicity?”; https://www.usgs.gov/faqs/can-position-moon-or-planets-affect-seismicity
confidence: No predictive evidence is asserted; see source for seismicity discussion.
